"'''You're So Vain'''" is a song by the American singer-songwriter [[Carly Simon]], released as a single in November 1972. The lyrics describe a self-absorbed lover, whose identity has long been a matter of speculation. Simon said the song refers to three men, one of whom she has named publicly—the actor [[Warren Beatty]].

Simon wrote "You're So Vain" over the course of a year. The song was originally titled "Bless You, Ben."<ref>{{cite web |last=Chagollan |first=Steve |date=April 9, 2012 |title=Deconstructing Carly Simon's 'You're So Vain' |url=https://variety.com/2012/music/news/deconstructing-carly-simons-youre-so-vain-29926/ |access-date=November 12, 2017 |website=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]}}</ref> The [[bass guitar]] introduction was played by [[Klaus Voormann]].<ref>{{cite web |date=1971-08-01 |title=Klaus Voormann : Biography |url=http://www.voormann.com/biography |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717231704/http://www.voormann.com/biography |archive-date=2011-07-17 |access-date=2014-05-30 |publisher=Voormann.com}}</ref> The strings were arranged by Simon and orchestrated by [[Paul Buckmaster]].

In early 1973, "You're So Vain" reached No. 1 in the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. In 1994, it was ranked 72nd in the ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' 50th anniversary all-time chart.<ref name="Billboard-1994">{{cite magazine |date=May 21, 1994 |title=Billboard Hot 100 All-Time Top Songs (80–71)  |url=http://www.billboard.com/bbcom/specials/hot100/charts/top100-titles-80.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080913210022/http://www.billboard.com/bbcom/specials/hot100/charts/top100-titles-80.shtml |archive-date=September 13, 2008 |magazine=Billboard |access-date=August 1, 2018}}</ref>  At the [[16th Annual Grammy Awards]] in 1974, it was nominated for [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year|Song of the Year]], [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]], and [[Grammy Award for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance|Best Female Pop Vocal Performance]]. It was voted No. 216 in [[Recording Industry Association of America|RIAA]]'s [[Songs of the Century]], and in August 2014, the UK's [[Official Charts Company]] named it the ultimate song of the 1970s. In 2021, the song was ranked 495th on [[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time]].

sections.heading: Lyrics
sections.wikitext:
Before Simon rewrote the lyrics, the song was titled "Bless You, Ben".<ref name="Chagollan-2012" /> She first rewrote the chorus lyric "You're so vain / You probably think this song is about you". A year later, she saw a man wearing a scarf arrive at a party and study himself in a mirror. A friend of Simon's said that "he looks like he's walking onto a yacht", inspiring the rest of the lyrics.<ref name="Chagollan-2012">{{cite web |last=Chagollan |first=Steve |date=April 9, 2012 |title=Deconstructing Carly Simon's 'You're So Vain' |url=https://variety.com/2012/music/news/deconstructing-carly-simons-youre-so-vain-29926/ |access-date=November 12, 2017 |website=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]}}</ref>

Simon used the word "[[gavotte]]", a French dance, as it provided a necessary rhyme and "that's what a pretentious, vain man would do".<ref name="Chagollan-2012" /> The line "They were clouds in my coffee" was inspired by a comment from her piano player, Billy Mernit, who observed that clouds were reflected in a cup of coffee she was drinking.<ref name="Chagollan-2012" />

The lyrics "Well, I hear you went up to [[Saratoga Springs, New York|Saratoga]], and your horse naturally won / Then you flew your [[Learjet]] up to [[Nova Scotia]], to see the total eclipse of the sun" may refer to the [[solar eclipse of March 7, 1970]], that was visible along the east coast of North America,<ref name="t1172">{{cite news |last=Carter |first=Jamie |date=2024-03-07 |title=54 Years Ago Today A Total Eclipse Of The Sun Inspired 'You're So Vain' |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/jamiecartereurope/2024/03/07/54-years-ago-today-a-total-eclipse-of-the-sun-inspired-youre-so-vain---history-repeats-in-32-days/ |access-date=2024-11-30 |website=Forbes |quote="The song’s iconic lyric, 'you flew your Learjet up to Nova Scotia to see the total eclipse of the sun' was motivated by events around a landmark eclipse that occurred exactly 54 years ago today, on March 7, 1970."}}</ref><ref name="p1672">{{cite web |last=Hendry |first=Glenn |date=2024-04-08 |title=A hit song's connection to the solar eclipse and Canada |url=https://www.insauga.com/a-hit-songs-connection-to-the-solar-eclipse-and-canada/ |access-date=2024-12-01 |website=INsauga |quote="What is not in dispute is the eclipse she was referring to, which happened on March 7, 1970."}}</ref> or the [[solar eclipse of July 10, 1972]], which was only visible in northern and eastern Canada.<ref name="z8952">{{cite book |last=English |first=L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jXc3EAAAQBAJ&pg=PA92 |title=More than Music: Cultural Stirrings From Pink Floyd's 'The Dark Side of the Moon' |publisher=Algora Publishing |year=2021 |isbn=978-1-62894-442-6 |page=92 |quote="Her song was released only four months after an actual total eclipse visible in Nova Scotia on July 10, 1972.... So it remains an enigma of which eclipse she meant and how she knew to write about it. |access-date=2024-12-28}}</ref> Simon told the [[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation|CBC]] that she took artistic license with the reference, and the subject may not have actually witnessed the eclipse in [[Nova Scotia]].<ref name="h324">{{cite news |last=Woodbury |first=Richard |date=2024-04-05 |title=With eclipse in sight, Carly Simon talks name-dropping Nova Scotia in You're So Vain |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/nova-scotia/carly-simon-interview-nova-scotia-1.7164465 |access-date=2024-11-30 |website=CBC |quote="As for the mystery man who flew his Learjet to Nova Scotia to see an eclipse, Simon said she took certain liberties for artistic reasons."}}</ref> In the 2012 biography ''More Room in a Broken Heart: The True Adventures of Carly Simon'', she stated: "I didn't know anyone who raced at Saratoga or went to view the total eclipse of the sun. I just wanted to portray someone who thought he was ultra-cool."<ref name="v9752">{{cite book |last=Davis |first=Stephen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xz_ZCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA207 |title=More Room in a Broken Heart: The True Adventures of Carly Simon |publisher=Penguin Publishing Group |year=2013 |isbn=978-1-59240-743-9 |page=207 |access-date=2024-12-01}}</ref>
sections.text:
Before Simon rewrote the lyrics, the song was titled "Bless You, Ben". She first rewrote the chorus lyric "You're so vain / You probably think this song is about you". A year later, she saw a man wearing a scarf arrive at a party and study himself in a mirror. A friend of Simon's said that "he looks like he's walking onto a yacht", inspiring the rest of the lyrics.

Simon used the word "gavotte", a French dance, as it provided a necessary rhyme and "that's what a pretentious, vain man would do". The line "They were clouds in my coffee" was inspired by a comment from her piano player, Billy Mernit, who observed that clouds were reflected in a cup of coffee she was drinking.

The lyrics "Well, I hear you went up to Saratoga, and your horse naturally won / Then you flew your Learjet up to Nova Scotia, to see the total eclipse of the sun" may refer to the solar eclipse of March 7, 1970, that was visible along the east coast of North America, or the solar eclipse of July 10, 1972, which was only visible in northern and eastern Canada. Simon told the CBC that she took artistic license with the reference, and the subject may not have actually witnessed the eclipse in Nova Scotia. In the 2012 biography More Room in a Broken Heart: The True Adventures of Carly Simon, she stated: "I didn't know anyone who raced at Saratoga or went to view the total eclipse of the sun. I just wanted to portray someone who thought he was ultra-cool."

sections.heading: Subject
sections.wikitext:
[[File:Warren Beatty Photoplay, 1961.jpg|thumb|Simon confirmed that the actor [[Warren Beatty]] (pictured in 1961) was one inspiration for the lyrics.]]
In 1972, Simon told an interviewer that the song was about "men", not a specific man.<ref name="vffun" /> In 1983, she said it was not about [[Mick Jagger]],<ref name="wapo">{{cite news |last=Wadler |first=Joyce |date=October 30, 1983 |title=Carly Simon: Anxiety & |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/style/1983/10/30/carly-simon-anxiety-38/16c584f8-6e76-4350-821d-9e02f18d92f2/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305083601/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/style/1983/10/30/carly-simon-anxiety-38/16c584f8-6e76-4350-821d-9e02f18d92f2/ |archive-date=2016-03-05 |access-date=November 28, 2021 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref> who contributed uncredited [[Backing vocalist|backing vocals]] to the song<ref name="allmusicbio">{{cite web | url=http://www.allmusic.com/artist/carly-simon-mn0000147635/biography|title=Carly Simon Biography |first= William|last= Ruhlmann| publisher=[[AllMusic]] | access-date= 2015-11-18}}</ref> (Simon said she invited him to join the recording when he made a call into the studio.<ref>{{cite web |last=Giles |first=Jeff |date=January 6, 2014 |title=When Carly Simon and Mick Jagger Topped the Charts With "You're So Vain" |url=https://ultimateclassicrock.com/carly-simon-mick-jagger-youre-so-vain/ |access-date=September 30, 2019 |website=[[Ultimate Classic Rock]] |publisher=}}</ref>) In a 1993 book, [[Angie Bowie]] said she was the "wife of a close friend" mentioned in the song, and that Jagger had been "obsessed" with her.{{Clarify|reason=Who is "her"?|date=September 2025}}<ref>''Backstage Passes''</ref>

Simon appeared as a guest artist on [[Janet Jackson]]'s 2001 single "[[Son of a Gun (I Betcha Think This Song Is About You)]]", which [[Sampling (music)|sampled]] "You're So Vain". In "Son of a Gun", Simon recites the lines "The apricot scarf was worn by Nick / Nothing in the words referred to Mick."<ref name="Friedman-2015">{{Cite web |last=Friedman |first=Megan |date=2015-11-18 |title=Carly Simon Finally Reveals Who "You're So Vain" Is About |url=https://www.redbookmag.com/life/a41019/carly-simon-youre-so-vain-warren-beatty/ |access-date=2020-06-14 |website=Redbook |language=en-US}}</ref> "Nick" is the novelist [[Nicholas Delbanco]], whom Simon dated in the 1960s.<ref name="Friedman-2015" /> Simon also denied that the song was about her ex-husband [[James Taylor]].<ref name="Rolling Star2">{{cite magazine |date=1973-01-04 |title=James Taylor and Carly Simon: The Rolling Stone Interview |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/james-taylor-and-carly-simon-the-rolling-stone-interview-228269/ |access-date=2018-11-30 |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]}}</ref> [[David Bowie]], [[David Cassidy]] and [[Cat Stevens]] have been cited by the press as other possibilities.<ref name="njstar2">{{cite web |date=2010-02-27 |title='You're So Vain': Carly Simon reveals mystery man |url=http://www.nj.com/entertainment/index.ssf/2010/02/youre_so_vain_carly_simon_reve.html |access-date=2016-10-08 |website=NJ.com}}</ref><ref name="nydn2">{{cite news |last=Roberts |first=Soraya |date=2010-02-27 |title=Carly Simon's new 'You're So Vain' whispers clue |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/entertainment/music/2010/02/27/2010-02-27_chinese_whisper_new_recording_of_carly_simons_youre_so_vain_offers_up_david_as_i.html |access-date=2016-10-08 |newspaper=[[New York Daily News]]}}</ref><ref name="cnnclue2">{{cite web |author=Sosa |first=Ninette |title=Carly Simon reveals 'You're So Vain' clue |url=https://www.cnn.com/2010/SHOWBIZ/Music/02/26/carly.simon.so.vain/index.html |access-date=2016-10-08 |website=[[CNN]]}}</ref>

In August 2003, Simon agreed to reveal the subject to the highest bidder of the [[Martha's Vineyard]] Possible Dreams charity auction. The highest bid was $50,000 from Simon's friend [[Dick Ebersol]], the president of [[NBC Sports]]. A condition of the prize was that Ebersol not reveal the name.<ref name="USAToday">{{cite web |date=August 5, 2003 |title=Carly Simon gives away who is 'So Vain' |url=https://www.usatoday.com/life/music/news/2003-08-05-simon-vain_x.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130818180418/http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/life/music/news/2003-08-05-simon-vain_x.htm |archive-date=August 18, 2013 |agency=[[Associated Press]] |website=[[USA Today]]}}</ref> Simon allowed him to divulge a clue, and he said the person's name contained the letter E.<ref>Ebersol on NBC's ''Today'', August 5, 2003.</ref> In 2004, Simon said the name also contained the letters A and R.<ref name="a, e, and r">{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b833E40Iw5M&t=13a |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/b833E40Iw5M |archive-date=2021-12-21 |url-status=live|title=Regis & Kelly 2004 – Carly Simon talks about You're So Vain |publisher=[[YouTube]] |date=2012-09-08 |access-date=2016-10-08}}{{cbignore}}</ref> In 2005, Simon's ex-husband, Jim Hart, said he was sure the song was not about anyone famous.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://rulefortytwo.com/secret-rock-knowledge/chapter-10/carly-simon-youre-so-vain/ |title=I've heard a million different stories—who was Carly Simon actually singing about in "You're So Vain"? |publisher=Rule Forty Two |access-date=2016-10-08}}</ref>

In her 2008 book ''Girls Like Us'', Sheila Weller includes a detailed account of Simon's love affair with the musician [[Dan Armstrong]], suggesting that he was the inspiration. However, Simon's heartbreak over losing him inspired the song "Dan, My Fling", which appeared on her first album.<ref>Sheila Weller. ''Girls Like Us: Carole King, Joni Mitchell, and Carly Simon & the Journey of a Generation'', Simon & Schuster. 2008: {{ISBN|978-0-7434-9147-1}}</ref>  After her 2014 interview on his radio show, [[Howard Stern]] said Simon had privately revealed the identity to him, saying, "There is an odd aspect to it... He's not that vain." He also said it was a composite of three people.<ref name="howardstern">{{cite episode |series=Howard Stern Show |last=Stern |first=Howard (host) |network=Sirius XM Radio |date=May 20, 2014}}</ref> Simon confirmed that she had given the names to a few people, including Stern.<ref>{{cite web
| url        = https://www.bbc.com/news/entertainment-arts-34866406
| title      = Carly Simon: You're So Vain is about Beatty and two others
| work       = BBC
| date       = 2015-11-19
| access-date = 2017-08-31
}}</ref>

In an interview for [[WNYC]] in November 2009, Simon said she had hidden the name of the subject in a new recording of the song. thumb|Simon confirmed that the actor [[Warren Beatty (pictured in 1961) was one inspiration for the lyrics.]]
In 1972, Simon told an interviewer that the song was about "men", not a specific man. In 1983, she said it was not about Mick Jagger, who contributed uncredited backing vocals to the song (Simon said she invited him to join the recording when he made a call into the studio.) In a 1993 book, Angie Bowie said she was the "wife of a close friend" mentioned in the song, and that Jagger had been "obsessed" with her.{{Clarify|reason=Who is "her"?|date=September 2025}}

Simon appeared as a guest artist on Janet Jackson's 2001 single "Son of a Gun (I Betcha Think This Song Is About You)", which sampled "You're So Vain". In "Son of a Gun", Simon recites the lines "The apricot scarf was worn by Nick / Nothing in the words referred to Mick." "Nick" is the novelist Nicholas Delbanco, whom Simon dated in the 1960s. Simon also denied that the song was about her ex-husband James Taylor. David Bowie, David Cassidy and Cat Stevens have been cited by the press as other possibilities.

In August 2003, Simon agreed to reveal the subject to the highest bidder of the Martha's Vineyard Possible Dreams charity auction. The highest bid was $50,000 from Simon's friend Dick Ebersol, the president of NBC Sports. A condition of the prize was that Ebersol not reveal the name. Simon allowed him to divulge a clue, and he said the person's name contained the letter E. In 2004, Simon said the name also contained the letters A and R. In 2005, Simon's ex-husband, Jim Hart, said he was sure the song was not about anyone famous.

In her 2008 book Girls Like Us, Sheila Weller includes a detailed account of Simon's love affair with the musician Dan Armstrong, suggesting that he was the inspiration. However, Simon's heartbreak over losing him inspired the song "Dan, My Fling", which appeared on her first album.  After her 2014 interview on his radio show, Howard Stern said Simon had privately revealed the identity to him, saying, "There is an odd aspect to it... He's not that vain." He also said it was a composite of three people. Simon confirmed that she had given the names to a few people, including Stern.

In an interview for WNYC in November 2009, Simon said she had hidden the name of the subject in a new recording of the song. In 2010, a representative for Simon said the name was "David". Media outlets speculated that the subject was the Elektra Records executive David Geffen. Hart immediately downplayed this. Simon later claimed she had not met Geffen when she wrote the song in 1971. Simon's publicist confirmed the song was not about Geffen, but that there was "a David who is connected to the song in some way, shape, or form". Vanity Fair noted that in addition to "David", "Warren" and an unintelligible name are whispered in the song. After her performance of the song with Simon in July 2013, the songwriter Taylor Swift said that Simon had revealed the identity of the subject to her in confidence.

In 1983, Simon said the actor Warren Beatty "certainly thought it was about him—he called me and said thanks for the song". In 2007, Beatty said, "Let's be honest. That song was about me."  In November 2015, Simon, promoting her memoirs, said, "I have confirmed that the second verse is Warren ... Warren thinks the whole thing is about him ... Now, that doesn't mean that the other two verses aren't also about Warren. It just means that the second one is." The song originally had a fourth verse, possibly including another subject.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext:
Reviewing the single, ''[[Record World]]'' called it Simon's "most commercial song yet", praising the lyrics, melody and string arrangements.<ref name="rw">{{cite magazine |date=November 25, 1972 |title=Hits of the Week |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/70s/72/RW-1972-11-25.pdf |magazine=Record World |page=1 |accessdate=2023-03-28}}</ref> At the [[16th Annual Grammy Awards]] in 1974, "You're So Vain" was nominated for [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year|Song of the Year]], [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]], and [[Grammy Award for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance|Best Female Pop Vocal Performance]].

In 1994, "You're So Vain" was ranked 72nd in the ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' 50th anniversary all-time chart.<ref name="Billboard-1994" /> It was voted No. 216 in [[Recording Industry Association of America|RIAA]]'s [[Songs of the Century]],<ref>{{cite web |date=March 7, 2001 |title=Songs of the Century |url=http://edition.cnn.com/2001/SHOWBIZ/Music/03/07/list.top.365.songs/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211082620/https://edition.cnn.com/2001/SHOWBIZ/Music/03/07/list.top.365.songs/ |archive-date=February 11, 2024 |access-date=March 9, 2013 |work=[[CNN]]}}</ref> and in 2014 the UK [[Official Charts Company]] named it the ultimate song of the 1970s.<ref>{{cite web |last=Myers |first=Justin |date=2014-08-23 |title=Official Charts Pop Gem #70: Carly Simon – You're So Vain |url=http://www.officialcharts.com/features/official-charts-pop-gem-70-carly-simon-youre-so-vain-3071/ |access-date=2016-10-08 |website=Officialcharts.com}}</ref> In 2021, it was ranked 495th on [[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time]].<ref>{{cite magazine |date=September 15, 2021 |title=The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-songs-of-all-time-1224767/carly-simon-youre-so-vain-1224842/ |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]}}</ref> In June 2026, [[CBS News]] included the song in its list of the 250 most essential American songs of the past 250 years.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Essential American Songbook |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/projects/2026/sunmo-american-songbook/ |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en}}</ref>
sections.text:
Reviewing the single, Record World called it Simon's "most commercial song yet", praising the lyrics, melody and string arrangements. At the 16th Annual Grammy Awards in 1974, "You're So Vain" was nominated for Song of the Year, Record of the Year, and Best Female Pop Vocal Performance.

In 1994, "You're So Vain" was ranked 72nd in the Billboard 50th anniversary all-time chart. It was voted No. 216 in RIAA's Songs of the Century, and in 2014 the UK Official Charts Company named it the ultimate song of the 1970s. In 2021, it was ranked 495th on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. In June 2026, CBS News included the song in its list of the 250 most essential American songs of the past 250 years.

sections.heading: Sales
sections.wikitext: The song was a No. 1 hit in the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, and reached No 4 in Ireland and South Africa.<ref>{{cite web|author=Brian Currin |url=http://rock.co.za/files/springbok_top_20_(S).html |title=South African Rock Lists Website – SA Charts 1965 – 1989 Acts (S) |website=Rock.co.za |access-date=2016-10-08}}</ref> Entering at No. 99 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] on 2 December 1972, the song took five more weeks to rise to the top of the chart, where it stayed for the first three weeks of 1973. It was replaced by [[Stevie Wonder]]'s "[[Superstition (song)|Superstition]]" and spent the next month in the runner-up spot. It also spent two weeks at the top of the [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Easy Listening]] chart in early 1973, her first No. 1 on either chart. "You're So Vain" was Simon's breakthrough hit in the United Kingdom, reaching No. 3 on the UK chart on its original release in 1973.
sections.text: The song was a No. 1 hit in the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, and reached No 4 in Ireland and South Africa. Entering at No. 99 on the Billboard Hot 100 on 2 December 1972, the song took five more weeks to rise to the top of the chart, where it stayed for the first three weeks of 1973. It was replaced by Stevie Wonder's "Superstition" and spent the next month in the runner-up spot. It also spent two weeks at the top of the Easy Listening chart in early 1973, her first No. 1 on either chart. "You're So Vain" was Simon's breakthrough hit in the United Kingdom, reaching No. 3 on the UK chart on its original release in 1973.
